title: Maximum acceptable toxicant concentration
wikitext:
{{more citations needed|date=March 2015}}

The '''maximum acceptable toxicant concentration''' (MATC) is a value that is calculated through [[Aquatic Toxicology|aquatic]] toxicity tests to help set [[water quality]] regulations for the protection of aquatic life. Using the results of a partial life-cycle [[chronic toxicity]] test, the MATC is reported as the [[geometric mean]] between the No Observed Effect Concentration ([[No-observed-adverse-effect level|NOEC]]) and the lowest observed effect concentration ([[Lowest-observed-adverse-effect level|LOEC]]).<ref name="Rand1">Rand, Gary (1995). ''Fundamentals of Aquatic Toxicology''. Boca Raton: CRC Press. pp. 943. {{ISBN|1-56032-090-7}}.</ref>

The MATC is used to set regulatory standards for priority pollutants<ref name="EPAPP">U.S. EPA. ''Priority Pollutants'' [https://www.epa.gov/cwa-methods].</ref> under the US federal [[Clean Water Act]]. Regulatory guidelines give two acceptable concentrations of pollutants to protect against effects: chronic or acute. Since the MATC should only be reported in chronic toxicity tests, there is a widely accepted method to convert the chronic MATC to a concentration that protects against acute effects.<ref name="Rand1"/>

The MATC is calculated and reported from the results of a number of standard procedures designed by the United States [[United States Environmental Protection Agency|Environmental Protection Agency]] (US EPA) and other organizations to maintain high [[accuracy and precision]] among all toxicity tests for regulatory purposes.

==Calculation==

===Chronic toxicity tests===
In a toxicity test, the NOEC and LOEC are derived as a comparison from the [[Scientific control|negative control]], or the experimental group that does not contain the chemical in question. The NOEC is the highest concentration that does not cause a statistically different effect than the negative control through [[statistical hypothesis testing]]. Likewise, the LOEC is the lowest concentration tested that does cause a statistically different effect than the negative control. The MATC is the geometric mean between these two values, such that: MATC={{math|{{radical|(NOEC)(LOEC)}}}}

The MATC is calculated to protect against chronic effects on overall function or health of an organism, not death. A partial life cycle test must be used. This type of toxicity test uses organisms in their most sensitive life stages, usually during times of early reproduction and growth, but not juveniles.<ref name="Rand2">Rand, Gary (1995). ''Fundamentals of Aquatic Toxicology''. Boca Raton: CRC Press. pp. 42-43. {{ISBN|1-56032-090-7}}.</ref> The MATC is the highest concentration that should not cause chronic effects, however, for regulatory purposes, a maximum concentration to protect against acute effects must exist as well.

===Applying MATC to acutely toxic concentrations===
The MATC can be applied to the results of an [[acute toxicity]] test to obtain a concentration that would protect against adverse effects during an acute exposure. An [[Median lethal dose|LC<sub>50</sub>]], or the concentration at which 50% of the organisms die during an acute toxicity test is used to derive a value called the acute to chronic ratio (ACR).

The MATC can be used to calculate the ACR as follows: <math> ACR= LC50/MATC </math>

The ACR is useful for estimating an MATC for species in which only acute toxicity data exists, or for setting regulatory guidelines for the protection of aquatic life through water quality criteria by the US EPA.<ref name="Rand2"/>

==Regulatory uses==

===United States===
The US EPA is the governmental organization responsible for writing and enforcing environmental regulations passed by Congress. The [[Clean Water Act]] was passed in 1972.

Section 304(a)(1) of the Clean Water Act is the Water Quality Criteria (WQC) developed for the protection of aquatic life and human health.<ref name="EPAWQC">U.S. E.P.A. ''Water Quality Criteria'' [https://web.archive.org/web/20110513155208/http://water.epa.gov/scitech/swguidance/standards/criteria/index.cfm].</ref> The MATC and ACR are used in a sequence of calculations to obtain the Criterion Maximum Concentration and Criterion Continuous Concentration (CMC and CCC, respectively) for the chemicals being regulated.<ref name="CCCCMC">U.S. EPA. ''CMC and CCC'' [https://www.epa.gov/wqc/national-recommended-water-quality-criteria-aquatic-life-criteria-table].</ref>

The CMC and CCC are two of the six parts of the aquatic life criterion under the WQC, and are the actual regulatory values for all priority pollutants tested. The CMC is the highest concentration of a chemical in water that aquatic organisms can be exposed to acutely without causing an adverse effect. Likewise, the CCC is the highest concentration of a chemical in water that aquatic organisms can be exposed to indefinitely without resulting in an adverse effect. Typically, the CMC is higher than the CCC.<ref name="CCCCMC"/>

===Canada===
[[Environment Canada]] is the regulatory agency for environmental protection in Canada. Under the Canada Water Act of 1970, the Canadian Water Quality Guidelines (CWQG) for the Protection of Aquatic Life give regulatory guidelines of maximum concentrations of pollutants that are acceptable in freshwater and marine environments.<ref name="CCME">Canadian Water Quality Guidelines. ''CCME Guidelines for the protection of aquatic life.'' {{cite web |url=http://www.waterquality.ec.gc.ca/waterqualityweb/guidelines.aspx?catId=1 |title=Archived copy |access-date=2013-05-31 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070823234813/http://www.waterquality.ec.gc.ca/waterqualityweb/guidelines.aspx?catId=1 |archive-date=2007-08-23 }}.</ref>

The CWQG's long and short-term exposure concentrations are derived in a similar way as the methods used by the US EPA, and are the CMC or CCC equivalents.<ref name="CCMEDERV">Canadian Council of Minister of the Environment. ''A Protocol for the Derivation of Water Quality Guidelines for the Protection of Aquatic Life 2007'' [ceqg-rcqe.ccme.ca/download/en/220/]</ref> When an MATC is reported with toxicity tests, it has sometimes been called a threshold-observed-effect-concentration (TOEC). The MATC and TOEC are both calculated as the geometric mean of the NOEC and LOEC, and are often used interchangeably.<ref name="CCMEDERV"/><ref name="CASTAT">Environment Canada (2005). ''Guidance Document on Statistical Methods for Environmental Toxicity Tests.'' pp. 113. EPS 1/RM/46</ref>

===Standard methods===

Standard methods are designed and used widely to maximize precision and accuracy for all toxicity tests. Values derived from toxicity tests such as the MATC are reported to regulatory organizations like the US EPA and Environment Canada so more confident regulations can be designed.{{citation needed|date=March 2015}}

Some common standard methods include those designed by the governmental organizations like Environment Canada, the US EPA, or the United States [[Food and Drug Administration|Food and Drug Administration (FDA)]]. Others are designed by scientific organizations such as [[ASTM International]], or the [[OECD]].

Many of these methods use the same test organism or are designed for the same exposure time. Common test organisms include, but are not limited to, [[daphnia]], [[fathead minnow]], [[rainbow trout]], and [[mussel]]s. Acute toxicity tests are normally 24–96 hours, whereas chronic tests will typically run for a week or longer.

==Advantages and limitations==

Using the MATC to derive regulatory guidelines has been accompanied with some debate. Hypothesis testing, or statistical tests performed with data sets that only report a significant difference, are not considered the most statistically robust. There are no confidence intervals to show a measure of uncertainty in a NOEC and LOEC. In addition, the NOEC and LOEC can only be concentrations in the test, and nothing in between.<ref name="RAND3">Rand, Gary (1995). ''Fundamentals of Aquatic Toxicology''. Boca Raton: CRC Press. pp. 86-87. {{ISBN|1-56032-090-7}}</ref> Because of these reasons, values that are derived through [[curve fitting]] methods, such as an LC50, or EC10 (the concentration that causes the measured effect in 10% of organisms) would be preferred if it was possible more often.

From a regulatory standpoint, there are advantages to using results from hypothesis tests. NOEC and LOEC's were used more often in the past, and there are more test results reporting NOEC and LOEC's than EC10's. The time and effort required to perform all of the previous tests to derive a different value is not seen as a good use of resources. In addition, the use of NOEC and LOEC's allows for reporting of one number to regulatory agencies.<ref name="CASTAT"/> Water Quality Criteria are reported as one number that the actual concentration must remain below. If the MATC were reported as a range of values to account for uncertainty, the regulatory guidelines would not be presented as a single value.

==One Health Implications==

The Maximum Acceptable Toxicant Concentration is a critical benchmark within the One Health framework, which emphasizes the fundamental interconnectedness of human, animal, and [[environmental health]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last1=Pesce |first1=Stéphane |last2=Ghiglione |first2=Jean-François |last3=Topp |first3=Edward |last4=Martin-Laurent |first4=Fabrice |date=2020-06-26 |title=Editorial: Microbial Ecotoxicology |journal=Frontiers in Microbiology |language=English |volume=11 |article-number=1342 |doi=10.3389/fmicb.2020.01342  |doi-access=free|issn=1664-302X |pmc=7333374 |pmid=32676059 |bibcode=2020FrMic..1101342P }}</ref> Although the MATC is technically derived from aquatic chronic toxicity data, its application in modern regulatory science provides a trans-disciplinary bridge between environmental monitoring and the protection of global health security.<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal |last1=Lin |first1=M.S. |last2=Varunjikar |first2=M.S. |last3=Lie |first3=K.K. |last4=Søfteland |first4=L. |last5=Dellafiora |first5=L. |last6=Ørnsrud |first6=R. |last7=Sanden |first7=M. |last8=Berntssen |first8=M.H.G. |last9=Dorne |first9=J.L.C.M. |last10=Bafna |first10=V. |last11=Rasinger |first11=J.D. |date=December 2023 |title=Multi-tissue proteogenomic analysis for mechanistic toxicology studies in non-model species |journal=Environment International |language=en |volume=182 |article-number=108309 |doi=10.1016/j.envint.2023.108309|doi-access=free |pmid=37980879 |bibcode=2023EnInt.18208309L |hdl=11250/3106445 |hdl-access=free }}</ref>

'''1. Integrated Risk Assessment'''

Contemporary toxicological research is shifting toward Integrated Risk Assessment, a model that evaluates chemical safety by linking environmental exposure directly to human health outcomes.<ref name=":2">{{Cite book |last=Oginah |first=Susan Anyango |url=https://orbit.dtu.dk/en/publications/integrated-risk-assessment-from-exposure-through-aops-to-ecosyste/ |title=Integrated risk assessment: from exposure through AOPs to ecosystem services |date=2023 |publisher=Technical University of Denmark |location=Kgs. Lyngby}}</ref> Because MATC values are calculated using sub-lethal chronic endpoints such as growth and reproduction, they provide essential biological data required for these integrated models;.<ref name=":2" /><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Wang |first1=Xiaolei |last2=Zhao |first2=Xiaoli |last3=Wang |first3=Ying |last4=Ruan |first4=Yuefei |last5=Liang |first5=Weigang |last6=Wu |first6=Fengchang |date=2024-12-13 |title=Human Health Water Quality Criteria: Research Challenges and Priorities |url=https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/acsestwater.4c00805 |journal=ACS ES&T Water |language=en |volume=4 |issue=12 |pages=5255–5263 |doi=10.1021/acsestwater.4c00805 |bibcode=2024ACSEW...4.5255W |issn=2690-0637|url-access=subscription }}</ref> This integrated approach allows scientists to better understand how low-level chemical concentrations in aquatic ecosystems can have cascading effects across the environment - animal - human interface.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Khan |first1=Mohiuddin Md Taimur |last2=Sklar |first2=Larry |date=2023-06-13 |title=Editorial: Environmental contaminants in aquatic systems and chemical safety for environmental and human health, volume II |journal=Frontiers in Public Health |language=English |volume=11 |article-number=1157834 |doi=10.3389/fpubh.2023.1157834  |doi-access=free|issn=2296-2565 |pmc=10299172 |pmid=37383263}}</ref>

'''2. Sentinel Species and Food Safety'''

In a One Health context, aquatic organisms serve as "sentinels" for emerging environmental hazards.<ref name=":1" /> For example, establishing chronic thresholds for persistent contaminants, such as per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, is a vital component of assessing chemical safety in shared water bodies;.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Melnyk |first1=Lisa Jo |last2=Lazorchak |first2=James M. |last3=Kusnierz |first3=Daniel H. |last4=Perlman |first4=Gary D. |last5=Lin |first5=John |last6=Venkatapathy |first6=Raghuraman |last7=Sundaravadivelu |first7=Devi |last8=Thorn |first8=Jonathan |last9=Durant |first9=James |last10=Pugh |first10=Katherine |last11=Stover |first11=Michael A. |date=2024 |title=One Health assessment of persistent organic chemicals and PFAS for consumption of restored anadromous fish. |journal=Journal of Exposure Science & Environmental Epidemiology |language=en |volume=34 |issue=6 |pages=1035–1044 |doi=10.1038/s41370-023-00620-3 |issn=1559-0631 |pmc=11541783 |pmid=38102302 |bibcode=2024JESEE..34.1035M }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Souza |first1=Marília Cristina Oliveira |last2=Barbosa |first2=Fernando |last3=Domingo |first3=Jose L. |date=2026-02-17 |title=PFAS and One Health: integrating human, animal, and environmental perspectives |journal=Archives of Toxicology |volume=100 |issue=5 |pages=1769–1787 |language=en |doi=10.1007/s00204-026-04306-1 |issn=0340-5761|doi-access=free |pmid=41699312 |pmc=13086820 |bibcode=2026ArTox.100.1769S }}</ref> Ensuring that environmental concentrations remain below the MATC for sensitive aquatic taxa is a primary preventative measure; it helps mitigate the [[bioaccumulation]] of toxins in fish and seafood, thereby protecting human populations from long-term health risks like immunotoxicity and cancer;.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Brambilla |first=Gianfranco |date=2024-05-06 |title=Safe and sustainable fish and seafood system and per- and poly-fluorinated substances occurrence: the role of PFAS toxicity in the assessment |url=https://link.springer.com/10.1007/s11356-024-33550-0 |journal=Environmental Science and Pollution Research |language=en |volume=31 |issue=22 |pages=33141–33147 |doi=10.1007/s11356-024-33550-0 |pmid=38709413 |bibcode=2024ESPR...3133141B |issn=1614-7499|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Polychronidou |first1=Vasiliki |last2=Nag |first2=Rajat |date=2025-10-20 |title=Human health risk assessment of Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) |journal=Science of the Total Environment |volume=1000 |article-number=180428 |doi=10.1016/j.scitotenv.2025.180428 |issn=0048-9697|doi-access=free |bibcode=2025ScTEn100080428P }}</ref>

'''3. Protection of Ecosystem Services'''

The One Health paradigm highlights that human well-being is dependent on "ecosystem services," such as clean drinking water, nutrient cycling, and biodiversity.<ref name=":3">{{Cite journal |last1=Maltby |first1=Lorraine |last2=Brown |first2=Ross |last3=Wilkinson |first3=Helen |date=2022-08-05 |title=Applying ecosystem services principles to the derivation of freshwater environmental quality standards |journal=Frontiers in Environmental Science |language=English |volume=10 |article-number=932161 |doi=10.3389/fenvs.2022.932161  |doi-access=free|bibcode=2022FrEnS..1032161M |issn=2296-665X|hdl=10871/130437 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> Benchmarks like the MATC are utilized to derive Environmental Quality Standards that specifically aim to protect the functional groups responsible for these services.<ref name=":3" /> By maintaining chemical levels below chronic effect thresholds, regulators safeguard the resilience of ecosystems that support human life and prevent environmental degradation;.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Barron |first1=Mace G. |last2=Otter |first2=Ryan R. |last3=Connors |first3=Kristin A. |last4=Kienzler |first4=Aude |last5=Embry |first5=Michelle R. |date=2021-03-05 |title=Ecological Thresholds of Toxicological Concern: A Review |journal=Frontiers in Toxicology |language=English |volume=3 |article-number=640183 |doi=10.3389/ftox.2021.640183  |doi-access=free|issn=2673-3080 |pmc=8915905 |pmid=35295098}}</ref><ref name=":0" />
